hypothesis: AI weather models such as GraphCast and Aurora, trained on diverse reanalysis and forecast datasets, already demonstrate superior skill in predicting climate-relevant extremes (atmospheric rivers, heat events) compared to traditional numerical weather prediction, and can be periodically retrained to track shifting climate patterns. By analogy with how language models are fine-tuned via parameter-efficient methods (e.g., LoRA) to adapt to new domains with minimal data, climate foundation models could adopt similar continual fine-tuning pipelines to rapidly assimilate non-stationary climate signals—such as accelerating sea-level rise or shifting jet-stream patterns—without full retraining. This cross-domain transfer of continual adaptation methodology could make AI-based climate forecasting systems self-updating sentinels for climate adaptation planning, dramatically reducing the latency between observed climate shifts and actionable forecast improvements.
